allow_large: Owner asked for this change (2026-10-09): pushing at start plus an optional Developer column in the story doc's parts table, read by task start, forge next and the board

amendments.because: Owner chose (2026-10-09): a lead plans stories first and assigns parts through an optional Developer column in the story's parts table; a mismatched start warns and is allowed
amendments.done_when: forge task start, forge fix start and forge story new push the new branch to GitHub as soon as it is made, so the branch is the claim and the author of its start commit is its owner; when the push fails the command says so plainly and the work stays local; task start's existing already-started refusal names the person who started the part on GitHub; the board page and forge board --json show who started each story, part and fix (from that start commit), next to the approver; no assignee field or roster is added; the coordinator guide says so; command tests cover a new repo and one adopted on an earlier release, including a second checkout refused with the first starter's name

done_when: forge task start, forge fix start and forge story new push the new branch to GitHub as soon as it is made, so the branch is the claim and the author of its start commit is its owner; when the push fails the command says so plainly and the work stays local; task start's existing already-started refusal names the person who started the part on GitHub. A story's parts table may carry an optional Developer column (a GitHub username) that the lead fills or changes below For the builders without a new approval; forge next shows a developer the parts assigned to them that can start, matched by their GitHub login; when someone other than the assigned developer starts a part, task start goes ahead and says who it was assigned to; the board page and forge board --json show for each story, part and fix its approver, its assigned developer when set, and who started it; story docs without the column work as today; no other assignee field or roster is added; the story template and coordinator guide describe the column; command tests cover a new repo and one adopted on an earlier release, including a second checkout refused with the first starter's name, an assigned part shown in that developer's forge next, and a warned start by someone else

findings.body: A teammate cannot discover their assigned ready parts before the first part merges, even after fetching the approved story branch. nextstep.py:363–383 discovers stories only from the default branch and local story worktrees, so the new login filter never sees that published plan. There is also a stale-assignment path: task start creates a local story branch only once (task.py:181–183), then reads it at lines 220–238 without incorporating subsequent updates pushed by the lead. Both boards likewise prefer that stale local plan (board.py:358–363 and story.py:388–398), so reassignment can leave next offering the previous developer's work, start warning about the previous developer, and the boards displaying the previous assignment. Read published story plans for teammate discovery and reconcile subsequent published assignments while preserving local edits. The assignment tests all run in the lead's checkout; cover discovery and published reassignment from a separate checkout for both client histories.
findings.title: Not done: Developer assignments must be discoverable and current in teammate checkouts

findings.body: New evidence beyond the start-tag retention ruling: a rejected initial push leaves the retention tag exclusively local. When the user subsequently runs the normal close flow, close.py:448–453 pushes only the branch, so the original start tag never reaches GitHub. After squash merging and branch cleanup (merge.py:118–138), a fresh observer has no reference to the original task or fix start commit, and both boards lose its started_by value. Story attribution can also disappear when its failed publication is recovered without another published reference retaining its start. Ensure later publication also publishes the retained original start reference. The rejected-push tests stop immediately after the failure, while the cleanup test starts with successful publication, so neither detects this supported recovery path.
findings.title: Publish the retained start reference when a failed start is later recovered

findings.body: After an unmerged fix is abandoned and its worktree and branches are deleted, its immutable start tag remains. fix_start's name selection at task.py:335–340 considers only branches and merged state, so starting the same slug selects the old name and creates a new worktree and commit. This update-ref then fails because its empty expected old value requires the tag to be absent. The command consequently aborts before publication and leaves newly created work behind. Restarting a removed story or task with the same branch name hits the same failure. Reserve retained names during name selection, or handle the collision before creating work, while preserving the original tags.
findings.title: Account for retained start tags before reusing an abandoned branch name

why: On a team, started work stays on the laptop where it began until its first close, so teammates can't see who is working on what and two developers can start the same part; no person is shown on any item. Owner decision 2026-10-09: starting is the claim, with git as the one record
